subject: Lebende Fremdsprache
title: Reading About Urban Loneliness
kernfrage: How do cities shape the way people connect — or fail to connect — with each other?

intro.body: In this worksheet you will read two short texts about loneliness in modern cities. Read each text carefully before you attempt the tasks. You do not need to look up every unfamiliar word — try to work out meaning from context.

sections.title: Text A: The Crowded Stranger
sections.throughline: Lesestrategien für nicht-fiktionale Texte: globales Verstehen, Informationen lokalisieren, implizite Bedeutungen erschließen. Die Schüler:innen sollen erkennen, dass Einsamkeit in Städten ein gesellschaftliches Paradox darstellt.
talking_points: Wie unterscheidet sich 'Einsamkeit' von 'Alleinsein'? Begriffsklärung vor der Lektüre.
Welche Lesestrategie hilft bei einem argumentativen Text — scanning, skimming oder close reading?
Inwiefern ist die Ich-Perspektive des Textes eine rhetorische Entscheidung des Autors?
extensions: Vergleich mit einem deutschsprachigen Zeitungsartikel zum selben Thema (kontrastive Lektüre).
Schüler:innen recherchieren Statistiken zur Einsamkeit in Österreich und präsentieren ihre Befunde.
Lektüre eines literarischen Textes (z. B. Ausschnitt aus einem zeitgenössischen Roman) mit ähnlichem Thema und Vergleich der Perspektiven.

blocks.prompt:
Read Text A below carefully.

---
**Text A: The Crowded Stranger**

I have lived in London for eleven years. My flat is on the fourth floor of a building with thirty-two other flats. I know the name of exactly one neighbour: a retired teacher called Margaret who once knocked on my door to ask if I had a spare light bulb. That was four years ago. I have not spoken to her since.

This is not unusual. A 2023 survey by a British mental health charity found that more than half of people living in large cities reported feeling lonely "often" or "always" — a figure that rises sharply among 18- to 34-year-olds, who are, paradoxically, the most digitally connected generation in history. We share photographs of our meals, broadcast our opinions to hundreds of followers, and scroll through other people's carefully curated happiness, yet a growing body of research suggests that the more time young adults spend on social media, the less satisfied they feel with their real-world relationships.

City planners in Amsterdam and Vienna have recently begun experimenting with what they call "social infrastructure": community gardens, deliberately small parks designed to encourage conversation, libraries with built-in cafés where sitting for hours without spending money is explicitly welcome. Whether these initiatives can undo decades of car-centred urban design — which pushed pedestrians off streets and replaced front porches with underground parking — remains an open question.

What strikes me most about urban loneliness is how invisible it is. On my morning commute I stand shoulder to shoulder with hundreds of people, earphones in, eyes down. We have collectively agreed to pretend the others do not exist. This is not rudeness; it is a coping mechanism for a world that sends us more human signals every day than our Stone Age brains were ever designed to process. The city does not make us lonely. It makes us overwhelmed — and overwhelmed people retreat.
---
blocks.answer_key: Reading and orientation task — no written answer required. Students read the text and familiarise themselves with its content before the analytical tasks that follow.
watch_outs: Manche Schüler:innen überspringen den Einführungstext oder lesen ihn zu flüchtig. Darauf hinweisen, dass spätere Aufgaben ohne genaue Lektüre nicht lösbar sind.
Den Begriff 'social infrastructure' vorentlasten, falls der Grundwortschatz der Klasse eingeschränkt ist.

blocks.prompt: Read the statements below. Decide whether each one is TRUE or FALSE according to Text A, and write one sentence from the text that justifies your answer.

statements: The writer has lived in their building for more than a decade.
The survey mentioned in the text found that older adults feel lonelier than young adults.
Amsterdam and Vienna are trying to redesign parts of their cities to encourage social contact.
According to the writer, people on public transport are rude to each other.
The writer believes that cities cause loneliness.

blocks.answer_key: 1. TRUE — "I have lived in London for eleven years." 2. FALSE — The text says the figure "rises sharply among 18- to 34-year-olds," meaning young adults feel lonelier than older ones. 3. TRUE — "City planners in Amsterdam and Vienna have recently begun experimenting with what they call 'social infrastructure'." 4. FALSE — The writer explicitly says "This is not rudeness; it is a coping mechanism." 5. FALSE — The writer concludes: "The city does not make us lonely. It makes us overwhelmed."
blocks.acceptable_reasoning: Für Statement 2 ist eine Fehlinterpretation häufig (siehe watch_outs). Akzeptiere jede Antwort, die erkennt, dass Jüngere höhere Einsamkeitswerte haben als ältere Kohorten.
watch_outs: Statement 2 ist eine häufige Falle: 'rises sharply among 18- to 34-year-olds' bedeutet, dass junge Erwachsene einsamer sind als ältere — der Gegensatz zu Erwartung. Schüler:innen verwechseln oft Subjekt und Referenzgruppe des Vergleichs.
Schüler:innen neigen dazu, die Begründung mit eigenen Worten zu formulieren statt eine Textstelle zu zitieren. Aufgabenstellung nochmals klären.

levels: Correct judgement based on text
Plausible but text evidence contradicts
Incorrect, no basis in text
Precise quotation directly supports judgement
Quotation relevant but indirect
Paraphrase or no quotation

blocks.prompt: Choose the best answer for each question according to Text A.

options.question: What is the main paradox that the writer describes?
choices: A) Cities have too many parks and not enough housing.
B) Young people are highly connected online but feel lonely in real life.
C) London is more expensive than Amsterdam or Vienna.
D) Retired people are the loneliest group in cities.

options.question: Why does the writer say people avoid eye contact on public transport?
choices: A) They are all looking at their phones for entertainment.
B) They dislike the other passengers.
C) Their brains cannot process so many social signals at once.
D) It is considered impolite in British culture.

options.question: What do the urban planning experiments in Amsterdam and Vienna have in common?
choices: A) They focus on building more underground car parks.
B) They aim to increase the number of shopping centres.
C) They create spaces that encourage people to spend time together.
D) They replace public transport with cycling lanes.

blocks.answer_key: Q1: B. Q2: C — "It is a coping mechanism for a world that sends us more human signals every day than our Stone Age brains were ever designed to process." Q3: C — The shared aim is creating 'social infrastructure' to encourage conversation and togetherness.
watch_outs: Bei Q1 wählen Schüler:innen oft D, weil der Anfang des Textes die Nachbarin Margaret erwähnt. Sie lesen nicht über den ersten Absatz hinaus, bevor sie antworten.
Bei Q2 ist A ein attraktiver Distraktor; das Handy wird jedoch nie erwähnt — sorgfältige Lektüre ist entscheidend.

sections.title: Text B: The Architecture of Connection
sections.throughline: Übergang von Textverstehen zu textübergreifendem Denken: Schüler:innen vergleichen Positionen zweier Texte, erkennen implizite Wertungen und entwickeln eine eigene begründete Haltung.
talking_points: Welche impliziten Annahmen macht Text B über die Rolle des Staates / der Stadtplanung?
Inwiefern ergänzen oder widersprechen sich die Argumentationen von Text A und Text B?
Was bedeutet es, Daten 'zu lesen' — wie beeinflusst die Herkunft einer Studie ihre Glaubwürdigkeit?
extensions: Schüler:innen erarbeiten eine eigene 'social infrastructure'-Idee für ihre Schule und präsentieren sie kurz auf Englisch.
Vertiefung: Analyse einer Infografik zu Einsamkeitsstatistiken (Medienkompetenz).
Kreatives Schreiben: kurzer Brief aus der Perspektive der Nachbarin Margaret.

blocks.prompt:
Now read Text B.

---
**Text B: The Architecture of Connection**

For most of human history, people did not choose their neighbours. They were born into communities — villages, neighbourhoods, extended families — where social contact was unavoidable rather than optional. Historians and sociologists increasingly argue that this enforced togetherness, uncomfortable as it sometimes was, built the social muscles that modern urban life has allowed to atrophy.

The good news, according to researchers at University College London, is that environments shape behaviour. When people cannot avoid each other — in a well-designed courtyard, a shared laundry room, or a slow lift — they tend to talk. Small talk leads to familiarity; familiarity reduces fear; reduced fear opens the door to genuine trust. The design of a building is, in this sense, a social policy.

This insight has influenced a wave of new housing projects across Northern Europe. In co-housing developments in Denmark and the Netherlands, residents typically have small private apartments but share kitchens, workshops, and gardens. Studies following residents over time report significantly lower rates of loneliness and higher satisfaction with daily life compared with equivalent populations in conventional housing. Critically, residents did not choose co-housing because they were already sociable people; many were shy or sceptical at first. The environment changed their behaviour.

Critics point out that co-housing remains expensive and available only to those who can afford it or who are lucky enough to enter a state-subsidised scheme. Social infrastructure, they warn, must not become another privilege of the affluent. The challenge, then, is to export the lessons of the co-housing courtyard into everyday urban design — bus shelters wide enough to have a conversation, benches that face each other, stairwells lit and decorated well enough that people do not rush through them.
---
blocks.answer_key: Orientation reading — no written answer required.
watch_outs: Das Wort 'atrophy' ist für viele unbekannt. Den Kontext nutzen: 'social muscles that ... allowed to atrophy' kann auch ohne Wörterbuch erschlossen werden.
Co-housing als Konzept kurz erläutern, falls die Klasse es nicht kennt.

blocks.prompt:
Answer the following questions about Text B in full sentences.

(a) According to Text B, what is the connection between building design and social behaviour? Use evidence from the text.

(b) What does Text B say about the people who moved into co-housing projects? Does this surprise you? Why / why not?

(c) What criticism of co-housing does the writer include, and how does the writer respond to this criticism?
blocks.answer_key: (a) The text argues that design shapes behaviour: when people are forced into contact (e.g. shared courtyards, slow lifts), small talk develops, which builds familiarity and trust. The writer states: "The design of a building is, in this sense, a social policy." (b) Many residents were initially shy or sceptical — they did not choose co-housing because they were already sociable. This is surprising (or should be noted as counterintuitive) because it suggests that personality is less important than environment. Accept personal responses that engage with this idea. (c) The criticism: co-housing is expensive and not accessible to all. The writer's response: urban planners should apply the same design principles (facing benches, wide bus shelters, etc.) to everyday public spaces so the benefits are not confined to the affluent.
blocks.acceptable_reasoning: Für (b) sind persönliche Reaktionen legitim, sofern sie auf den Text bezogen sind. Punkte für Textnähe und kohärente Begründung vergeben.
watch_outs: Schüler:innen beantworten (c) häufig nur den Kritik-Teil und vergessen die Antwort des Autors darauf — beide Teile der Frage explizit einfordern.
Bei (a) reicht es nicht, nur zu paraphrasieren; eine Textstelle soll explizit zitiert werden. Das ggf. nochmals betonen.

levels: All three sub-questions answered correctly with text evidence
Two sub-questions answered correctly
One or fewer answered correctly
Relevant quotations or close paraphrase integrated naturally
Some evidence given but not always directly relevant
No evidence; answers rely on general knowledge only
Accurate grammar and appropriate vocabulary; full sentences throughout
Mostly correct with minor errors that do not impede meaning
Frequent errors that make meaning unclear

blocks.prompt:
Both Text A and Text B deal with loneliness in cities, but they approach the topic from different angles.

In 8–10 sentences, compare the two texts. Consider:
- What is the main argument or perspective in each text?
- Do the authors agree or disagree about the causes of urban loneliness?
- Which text do you find more convincing, and why?

Use evidence from both texts to support your points.
blocks.answer_key: Model answer: Text A, written in the first person, focuses on the personal experience of urban loneliness and attributes it primarily to cognitive overload — the city overwhelms its inhabitants, causing them to withdraw. Text B takes a more analytical, historical view, arguing that modern urban design has destroyed the enforced togetherness of pre-modern communities and that redesigned environments can restore social connection. The authors broadly agree that the problem is structural rather than a personal failing, but Text A is more pessimistic, while Text B is cautiously optimistic about solutions such as co-housing and redesigned public spaces. Students should justify their preference with a specific argument (e.g. Text B provides empirical evidence from studies; Text A is more emotionally immediate and relatable). Accept any well-reasoned preference backed by textual reference. (Auf Deutsch: Akzeptiert werden alle gut begründeten Antworten, die beide Texte einbeziehen.)
blocks.acceptable_reasoning: Die persönliche Präferenz kann für beide Texte verteidigt werden — entscheidend ist die Qualität der Begründung und der Textbezug.
watch_outs: Schüler:innen tendieren dazu, die Texte nacheinander zusammenzufassen statt sie zu vergleichen — explizit auf Vergleichsformulierungen hinweisen (whereas, in contrast, both writers, unlike Text A …).
Viele vergeben die Aufgabe zu schnell in 4–5 Sätze; auf das Mindestformat (8–10 Sätze) hinweisen.
Häufiger Fehler: eigene Meinung ohne Textbezug ('I think cities are bad because...'). Einfordern, dass jeder Standpunkt mit einem Textzitat oder einer klar identifizierbaren Textstelle gestützt wird.

levels: Both texts systematically compared with clear similarities/differences identified
Some comparison but one text dominates; little explicit contrast
Texts treated separately with no genuine comparison
Specific evidence from both texts integrated and discussed
Evidence from one text only, or very general references
No textual evidence; based on memory or general knowledge
Personal stance clearly stated and well-reasoned
Stance stated but weakly justified
No clear stance or reasoning
Wide range of vocabulary and structures; errors rare and minor
Adequate range; some errors but meaning clear throughout
Limited range; errors frequently impede meaning
